turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, must you interrogate him so? It’s quite dreadful; a gentleman should be treated with a certain… deference. I simply *adore* his earnestness, and he is perfectly devoted to *me*.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Deference, my dear Gwendolen, is earned, not freely dispensed! And as for earnestness, I find it frequently a rather distressing characteristic in gentlemen who have not yet demonstrated a firm grasp of their social obligations. Pray tell me, Mr. Worthing, what family have your antecedents? I require a pedigree, not a pronouncement.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mama, really! Must you persist in this utterly barbaric line of questioning? I’ve already told you, I *am* engaged to Mr. Worthing, and his earnestness is quite charming, thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Gwendolen, my dear, your enthusiasm is, as always, touching, but it does not absolve me from my duties! Mr. Worthing, I must confess, I find your Belgrave Square address… somewhat unremarkable. One expects a gentleman of presumed breeding to possess a more distinguished residential history.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I… well, Belgrave Square is quite convenient, you see. My guardian, the late Sir William, always felt it was… a respectable location, and I’ve maintained the residence, naturally.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “Convenience, Mr. Worthing, is a quality I associate more with tradesmen than gentlemen! Maintaining a residence, you say? One maintains a reputation, sir, and I see no evidence that you have done so with any particular diligence. Tell me, do you at least possess landed property? A small estate, perhaps, in the country?”

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A small estate? Yes, well, I do have a… a house in the country, actually. It’s called… it’s called the Manor House, near… near an undisclosed location, you understand. It’s quite charming, I assure you!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: An undisclosed location, Mr. Worthing? Really! I find your evasiveness profoundly unsettling. It suggests a lack of candor, which, I assure you, is a most undesirable characteristic in a gentleman—or, indeed, a prospective son-in-law.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Must you interrogate the poor man so? I have already accepted Mr. Worthing's proposal, and I find his… *discretion* quite charming, actually.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Discretion, my dear Gwendolen, is a virtue best left to diplomats and scoundrels! Mr. Worthing's *discretion*, as he calls it, appears to be merely a euphemism for a regrettable deficiency in his ability to speak frankly. Now, Mr. Worthing, let us return to this 'Manor House' of yours – an undisclosed location, you claim? I insist you provide me with its precise coordinates, or I shall be forced to assume you have something to hide.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really, you are being utterly ridiculous! Mr. Worthing clearly understands the importance of privacy, and I find that quite admirable, actually. I believe we should proceed with the engagement as planned, don't you think?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Privacy, my dear Gwendolen, is a luxury afforded to those who have nothing to conceal! Mr. Worthing, I am beginning to suspect that this 'Manor House' exists only in the fertile landscape of your imagination. Pray, sir, do not insult my intelligence further by attempting to obfuscate the truth with such frivolous pronouncements.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My dear Lady Bracknell, I assure you, the Manor House is quite real! It's simply… a matter of family tradition to maintain a degree of privacy regarding its precise location. I can, of course, provide you with details, but I fear it would involve a rather lengthy explanation about… well, about the arrangements.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A 'lengthy explanation,' you say? Mr. Worthing, I find your evasiveness quite remarkable. I trust you are not attempting to imply that I am unfamiliar with the intricacies of family arrangements; I have navigated more complex genealogical webs than you could possibly imagine!

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Must you interrogate Mr. Worthing as if he were a common criminal? I've already declared my intentions, and I believe his assurances are perfectly satisfactory. Let us move on to discussing the wedding arrangements, shall we?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Wedding arrangements, my dear Gwendolen? One does not simply leap to wedding arrangements before establishing the foundations of a respectable lineage! Mr. Worthing, I am most anxious to ascertain the particulars of your parentage – a matter which, I must confess, you have thus far treated with a distressing lack of candour.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really, you’re being absolutely absurd! Mr. Worthing is perfectly suitable, and I am quite capable of forming my own judgements, thank you very much. I insist we proceed with discussing the floral arrangements – lilies, naturally.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My dear Lady Bracknell, I understand your concern, and I truly do want to be forthcoming. It's just that my origins… they are a rather peculiar story, and I fear I haven't quite the words to explain them adequately at present. Perhaps, if you'd allow it, I could write you a full account?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A written account, Mr. Worthing? How very convenient! It allows me time to digest your explanation at my leisure, and, naturally, to consult with my solicitor. I trust this account will be exceedingly detailed, and, above all, truthful.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, a detailed and truthful account is precisely what I intend to provide, Lady Bracknell. I wouldn't dream of misleading you, or anyone, especially concerning something so important. I shall begin drafting it immediately, and have it sent to you by post first thing tomorrow.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
